_comment: Which assumptions earn a question. The budget is a ceiling, not a quota: the tier gate decides whether anything is asked at all, and a brief that states everything blocking asks nothing. Confidence only orders what the gate already let through.

_tiers.blocking: the brief means nothing without it and no default is defensible
_tiers.consequential: a wrong value moves the envelope or the setbacks — correctable, but not cheaply
_tiers.defaultable: a convention covers it; wrong is visible and correctable on the gallery screen without a re-solve
_tiers.never: not a value a user could answer, or not this stage's field

_city_is_blocking: It was `defaultable` while nothing consumed it. Stage ② cannot select a setback ruleset without it, and a wrong ruleset is a wrong envelope rather than a wrong label — so an unrecognised city is now worth a question.
_ask_below: The gate. A tier's bar is the confidence under which it is worth interrupting for. 0.0 means never — no confidence can fall below it. `defaultable` sits there on purpose: parking at 0.65 and occupants at 0.7 are fine inferences, both visible in the assumption table and correctable later, and asking about them is how a clarifier turns into a form.
_rank: Tier gates first, then confidence sorts within the tier. A blocking coin-flip outranks a consequential one however the numbers fall.
_depends_on: F depends on P when F's value was read off P. Two uses, one graph. (1) Ceiling: no inference is more certain than its source, so F's confidence caps at the minimum over its assumed parents, transitively. (2) Collapse: if a parent is itself a guess, asking about F wastes a question the parent's answer would have settled. `floors` has two parents and caps by the lower of them.
_not_an_edge: `road edges` does NOT depend on `facing`, tempting as it looks. Answering which way the frontage points does not tell you which *other* side carries a road, so collapsing it into `facing` would silently retire a question that has no other way of being asked.
_budget: A ceiling on an already-gated set. Generous rather than tight, because ranking by root means one answer lifts everything derived from it — in practice the gate returns fewer than this.

questions.plot size: What size is the plot? Dimensions like 30x40 or an area like 1200 sqft both work.
questions.bedrooms: How many bedrooms do you need?
questions.facing: Which direction does the road-facing edge of the plot point?
questions.road edges: Which sides of the plot have a road? A corner plot has two.
questions.frontage: Which side of the plot faces the road — the shorter one or the longer one?
questions.road width: How wide is the road the plot faces? It sets both the FAR and how many floors you may build.
questions.floors: Ground floor only, or do you want an upper floor as well?
questions.city: Which city is the plot in? It decides which setback rules apply.
questions.occupants: How many people will be living here?
questions.vastu: How closely should the plan follow Vastu?
